claims.text: Coupled tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between mechanically induced oxide-film renewal and stress-assisted oxide breakdown.
Freshly exposed material rapidly forms a dense, passivating oxide.
The newly formed oxide temporarily suppresses corrosion.
Mechanical action repeatedly disrupts and removes the oxide film.
Repeated oxide formation and mechanical removal determine the overall degradation rate.
The initial alloy microstructure supports formation of a protective oxide in the corrosive environment.
Oxide reformation inhibits corrosion, whereas mechanical oxide disruption enhances corrosion by exposing unpassivated metal.
Net degradation is controlled by the balance between oxide-reformation kinetics and mechanical-removal kinetics.
Relative to static corrosion, local total degradation can decrease where oxide regeneration compensates for mechanical removal.
Tribo-corrosion increases the wear component relative to static corrosion.
The corrosion component under tribo-corrosion may decrease or remain similar to static corrosion if the regenerated oxide provides sufficient passivation.
The effect is expected to be moderate and strongly dependent on the relative rates of wear and oxide reformation.
The proposed behavior should hold under moderate wear when oxide reformation can keep pace with oxide removal.
The mechanism may fail at extremely high wear rates or when oxygen availability is too low for rapid oxide regeneration.
Very high temperatures may destabilize the protective oxide and cause corrosion to dominate degradation.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that mechanical oxide disruption enhances corrosion, and the boundary states that sufficiently high wear can make corrosion dominate, yet the falsification rule says that consistently higher corrosion at higher wear rates would invalidate the model. That observation could instead be an expected result when oxide removal outruns regeneration.

The hypothesis predicts a possible decrease in 'total degradation' relative to static corrosion only in unspecified local regions, while also adding a positive mechanical-wear component. It does not give a coherent directional prediction for specimen-level total degradation against the stated static baseline.
